r1.report.contribution: The paper offers a scope-based reconciliation of the Bayesian and error-statistical positions on prediction versus accommodation, restricted to selection cases (hypotheses picked from a space because they fit the data). It distinguishes the rigidly designated selected hypothesis H from the outcome-indexed proposition σ, 'whatever the search S returns is true'. It concedes the previous referee's point that P(σ|e) = P(H|e) (Prop. 1) and relocates the predictivist discount from the posterior to incremental confirmation. Because the priors differ, B(σ,e) = B(H,e)/ρ, where the 'reach factor' ρ = O(σ)/O(H). The formal centrepiece is Prop. 2. Under joint permutation symmetry of the prior and equivariance of S, the de re Bayes factor factorizes as B(H,e) = B(H,A) · B(H,e|A), where A is the event that S selects H. The first factor equals ρ and the second equals B(σ,e). So 'support beyond selection' is identified with confirmation relative to a background that includes the selection event. The algebra is correct; I checked Props. 1–2 and the table in §5. The paper then maps this decomposition onto three things: the local/global significance distinction, the Bayesian Occam factor in mass scans, and Mayo's 'nominal vs actual' error probabilities. It argues (§7) that reporting and reliance concern σ, because readers' priors attach to the reported finding as such. The idea is clever and clearly presented, and Prop. 2 is a tidy result. As it stands, however, the paper does not deliver the reconciliation it advertises: the privileged status of σ is unmotivated, the two-object framing collapses outside the symmetric case, and the error-statistical mapping is undermined by the paper's own §8 concession.
major: 1. The privileging of σ is unmotivated, and without a motivation the central thesis (T2) is close to trivial. Prop. 1 shows that σ and H coincide on every e-world, indeed on every A-world. Their confirmations therefore differ only because of σ's content outside A: σ = (H∧A) ∨ (σ∧¬A). For any target value p, one can construct a proposition X with X∧e ≡ H∧e and P(X) = p by adjoining or removing ¬e-worlds. Every such X has H's posterior and an essentially arbitrary Bayes factor. This is the structure behind Popper and Miller's (1983) argument about the 'deductive' and 'inductive' parts of a hypothesis, and behind the debate it provoked (Jeffrey 1984; Levi 1984; Redhead 1985; Dunn and Hellman 1986; Gemes 1997 on content parts). The paper engages none of it. That 'e confirms σ less than H' therefore reports nothing about e's bearing on anything in particular. It reports where σ's prior mass lies off the actual evidence. The paper's §9 answer to the gerrymandering worry ('it is a perfectly good set of worlds') misses the point. The worry is not that σ fails to be a proposition. It is that indefinitely many propositions share H's posterior, and confirmation ranks them arbitrarily. The only principled reason offered for singling out σ is the §7 reporting argument, so the whole significance of (T1)–(T3) rests on §7 (see point 5). The same problem affects §5's lottery-theorist comparison. There the 'disagreement de dicto' compares the confirmation of σ_S with that of a different proposition, σ_T. Predictivism, however, is a claim that the same content is supported differently under different histories. Showing that two different propositions are differently confirmed does not vindicate that claim.

2. Outside the symmetric case, the 'two objects' framing collapses into one object relative to two backgrounds, and the symmetric case does not describe the paradigm. Prop. 2's identification B(H,e|A) = B(σ,e) requires invariance of the joint credence over hypotheses and data under relabelling. Real mass scans violate this. Backgrounds fall steeply with mass, resolution and efficiency vary across the window, and theoretical priors are non-uniform (the Higgs case the paper invokes had mass constraints from electroweak fits). Condition (i) concerns the likelihoods as well as the prior, so the claim that 'uniform priors and equivariant algorithms are standard' is not enough. When symmetry fails, the paper takes B(H,e|A) as the general explicans of support beyond selection, and σ drops out. The general thesis then becomes: e's confirmation of the rigid H depends on whether A is counted as evidence or as background. That is not a scope distinction. It is a background-relativity thesis, and it belongs to the old-evidence literature (Glymour 1980; Garber 1983; Howson 1991 on counterfactual backgrounds; Christensen 1999; Eells and Fitelson 2000). In particular the paper owes an account of why A, rather than some other conjunct of e, should be backgrounded. By the chain rule any partition e = A ∧ R yields B(H,e) = B(H,A) · B(H,R|A), so the decomposition is privileged only by an independent argument that A is the 'used' part. That is precisely Worrall's use-novelty question, and the paper inherits it rather than answering it. The title, abstract and (T2)/(T3) should be restated to reflect that the de dicto formulation is a special case.

3. The §8 concession about confidence intervals vindicates objection (O1) rather than answering it. For an interval estimator, the paper grants that B(σ,e) ≈ 1: the de dicto proposition is unconfirmed. Mayo nonetheless regards the use-constructed interval as severely tested. Her verdict tracks the pre-data error rate of the procedure, which corresponds to a high P(σ), a firmness-type quantity. Three consequences follow. (a) It contradicts §4.2, where the paper insists that the prediction/accommodation dispute concerns increase in firmness rather than firmness. (b) The match between the global p-value and de dicto confirmation in the scan now looks like a feature of that example, not a structural allocation. (c) What is uniform across error-statistical verdicts on selected hypotheses is that they quantify over what the procedure would have output, that is, a procedure's error rate. That is exactly (O1)'s diagnosis: 'the familiar contrast between a conditional probability and an unconditional error rate'. The retreat to 'same object, different measure' rescues (T3) only by weakening 'the error statistician is right about σ' to 'the error statistician's numbers are about the procedure', which no party disputes. A stronger version of the paper would either find a single credal quantity that tracks severity in both the hunting and the estimator cases, or concede that (T3) is a claim about subject matter only and drop the 'reconciliation' framing.

4. The look-elsewhere mapping targets the wrong de dicto object, and the novelty claimed in §6 is largely the existing composite-versus-point distinction. The global p-value is P(Z_max ≥ z | background only), which is a test of the existential null ¬∃. It is not P(· | ¬σ). The paper's own approximation ('nearly so otherwise') hides the 'signal exists but the search missed it' component of ¬σ. Discovery claims in high-energy physics, and Mayo's own treatment of the Higgs in SIST (2018, Excursion 3), are existential: 'a new boson in this range'. They are not outcome-indexed claims of the form 'whatever the maximum is, is real'. The Bayesian Occam penalty attaching to the composite or existential alternative rather than the point hypothesis is standard (Jeffreys; Berger; Cousins 2017, whom the paper cites). The paper's numbers show B(∃,e) ≈ 4 and B(σ,e) ≈ 9.3. That is, σ adds nothing beyond ∃ except a power-dependent odds correction. If the existential hypothesis does all the work in the paradigm case, the apparatus of σ is redundant there. The 'de re/de dicto' gloss would then be a redescription of the specific-versus-existential contrast, whose bearing on the look-elsewhere effect has already been discussed in philosophy of science (R. Dawid 2015, 'Higgs Discovery and the Look Elsewhere Effect', Phil. Sci. 82; Staley 2017, Synthese 194). Separately, the equation of tail-area probabilities P(Z ≥ z | ·) with likelihood denominators is loose. A p-value is not a likelihood, and conditioning on the tail event rather than the exact datum can change Bayes factors by orders of magnitude (Berger and Sellke 1987; Berger and Delampady 1987). The 'sampling-terms' correspondence in §5 needs a careful statement or should be withdrawn.

5. The reporting argument (§7), which is the only principled ground for privileging σ, is underdeveloped and arguably mis-specified. (a) The argument requires readers whose prior is P(σ) before the data: their prior predictive expectation of the search's success, computed under their own model of the search's power. A reader who has that is a reader with a full prior over Ω and a model of S. Such a reader can use the reported likelihood function directly, so no double-counting arises. The argument therefore needs readers who hold σ-priors without the model that generates them, and it should say who these readers are and whether their priors are coherent. (b) A natural 'base rate for results this kind of analysis turns up' is post-threshold: the reliability of reported or claimed discoveries, a positive-predictive-value quantity (Ioannidis 2005; Efron's local false discovery rate). That base rate already incorporates data-type evidence, and combining it with B(σ,e) would double-count in the opposite direction. (c) Relatedly, the formal model has S always return a member of Ω. Actual discovery procedures report only above a threshold, and Gross and Vitells's trials factor depends on that threshold. Reliance concerns σ conditional on a report being made. This is the problem treated in the Bayesian literature on selected-parameter inference (A. P. Dawid 1994, 'Selection paradoxes of Bayesian inference'; Senn 2008; Yekutieli 2012; the 'winner's curse' literature), none of which is cited. (d) 'Science transmits support, not posteriors' is asserted rather than argued. Global p-values are not support measures that readers can multiply by priors, so the claim that the global significance is 'the frequentist counterpart' of the figure that 'combines correctly with a σ-prior' needs much more care.

6. The paper is not a reconciliation but a sophisticated Bayesian anti-predictivism, and it should be framed as one. On the question actually in dispute, whether the way H was found affects how strongly e supports H, (T1)/(T3) side with the Bayesian. §8 then concedes that Mayo's inference from low severity to 'x₀ is poor evidence for H' is to be rejected. Objection (O3) is therefore accepted, not answered. The §8 argument that Mayo's counterfactual is 'false on the rigid reading' also overlooks a reading available to her. In her framework the test that H passed is the hunting procedure. Applied rigidly to H_k, that procedure would, were H_k false, very probably output something else, and so 'accord less well with H_k'. On this reading severity comes out high, so Mayo cannot locate the low severity there. But this shows that her low-severity verdict and her conclusion about H_k are mismatched, which is a substantive criticism of her view, not a vindication of it. The paper should position itself in the weak/strong predictivism taxonomy (Hitchcock and Sober 2004; Barnes 2008, The Paradox of Predictivism; Barnes, SEP entry 'Prediction versus Accommodation'). It should also engage the many 'side-effect' Bayesian accounts that likewise locate the predictivist intuition in something other than H's support (Lange 2001; Lipton 2004 on fudging; Kahn, Landsberg and Stockman 1992; Kotzen 2012, 'Selection Biases in Likelihood Arguments', BJPS; Sober 2009/2011 on observation selection effects).

7. The claimed scope (§9: 'data dredging, model search, post hoc subgroup analysis') outruns the apparatus. Prop. 1 and the whole construction require S to be a deterministic function known to the agent, so that e entails A. In the dredging, forking-paths and p-hacking cases that motivate much of the selection literature (Gelman and Loken 2014), the reader does not know S, and S is not well defined. In those cases there is no σ whose prior the reader can compute, and the remedy practitioners use (pre-registration, holdout data) is justified on grounds the paper does not reach. The paper should either restrict its scope to algorithmic, publicly specified searches or extend the account to uncertainty about S.
minor: Internal numerical inconsistency. §8 describes the running example as a '5σ excess', but the §5 stipulations (B(H_k,e) ≈ 8000, B(σ,e) ≈ 9.3, n = 1000) correspond to a local excess of roughly 3.5–4σ and a weak global result. A genuine 5σ local excess (p ≈ 3×10⁻⁷) in 1000 cells has global p of order 10⁻⁴, and on the paper's own correspondence its de dicto likelihood ratio would be in the thousands, not about 9. Either change the description or rebuild the numbers.

(T2) as stated ('smaller, by a factor I call the reach') is false whenever ρ < 1, which §4.3 explicitly allows. Restate it as 'differs by the factor ρ, which exceeds 1 in searches over large undifferentiated spaces'. Note also that under the symmetry conditions ρ > 1 iff the search's power exceeds roughly 1/n (better than random selection). The 'reversal' cases therefore require asymmetric priors, and the claim that the account 'predicts' them is untested against any intuition or practice.

§4.2: the reach factor does not grow linearly in n at fixed resolution. Power of a max-statistic search declines as n grows, because the maximum of n noise cells grows roughly as √(2 log n). The claim 'a reach factor in the hundreds' for 1000 cells depends on the assumed power and should be stated as such.

§4.3 lists 'the likelihood-ratio measure' alongside the Bayes factor as if they were distinct. They are the same measure (Fitelson's l), so the robustness claim covers d, r and l (and also Crupi–Tentori's z). Since Fitelson 1999 concerns measure sensitivity, say explicitly that the ordinal result is robust but ρ itself is not.

§6: 'P(∃|e) ≈ P(H_k|e)' assumes negligible posterior mass on resonances in other cells; state this assumption. The 'price of 60% power' factor of 2.33 is O(∃)/O(σ), which depends on P(∃) as well as on power; describe it accurately.

Terminology. 'De re/de dicto' properly marks the scope of an attitude or modal operator relative to a description. What the paper uses is the contrast between a rigidly designated proposition and a non-rigid, outcome-indexed one (closer to two-dimensional or diagonal propositions). §9's remark that σ's 'content shifts with the data' is also misleading: σ is a fixed set of worlds; what shifts is which Hᵢ it agrees with at a world. The Smith/lottery analogy is apt, but the label invites confusion with the attitude-ascription literature.

§4.5's claim that 'neither school has made that claim' (that the procedure fixes the partition of a procedure-independent total evidential import) needs qualification in light of A. P. Dawid 1994, Yekutieli 2012 and the empirical-Bayes 'double use of data' literature. Scope the originality claim carefully.

§6: Scott and Berger (2010) concern multiplicity control via hyperpriors on inclusion probabilities in variable selection. The analogy to a single-resonance scan with a fixed uniform location prior is loose and should be flagged as such.

Worrall 2014 is cited for the 'cannot count twice' intuition, but the canonical statements of use-novelty are Worrall 1985, 1989 and 2002 (and Zahar 1973; Gardner 1982). Cite them. Mayo and Cox 2006 is a more direct source than Mayo 1996 for 'nominal vs actual' error probabilities under selection.

The characterization of White 2003 ('evidence of reliable theory construction') is roughly right, but White's argument concerns the theorist's reliable sensitivity to truth in theory choice. Since the paper claims these cases fall outside its scope, it should say precisely why they are not themselves selection cases, given that a theorist's choice is a selection from a space.

The manuscript is written as a response to a previous referee ('my original formulation', 'the referee's objection'). A journal submission must stand alone. Present (O1)–(O3) as objections in their own right and remove the revision narrative.

§7 replication: 'ρ = 1 for e′' should be stated carefully. Given e, σ ≡ H, so B(σ,e′|e) = B(H,e′|e) trivially. The interesting claim is about how the replication's support should be reported to readers whose priors attach to σ, and that claim needs the (contested) §7 machinery.

Formatting: the table in §5 uses a backslash-escaped pipe ('O(H_k \| e)'), which will render incorrectly. Several key formulas (the chain rule in Prop. 2, LR(e)/LR(A)) should be displayed and numbered for reference.

# Support Beyond Selection: The Prediction/Accommodation Dispute in Selection Cases

## 1. Introduction

Predictivism is the claim that evidence a hypothesis predicted supports it more than evidence the hypothesis was built or chosen to fit. Bayesians typically deny this (Howson and Urbach 2006). On their view the posterior P(H | e) is fixed by H's prior and by the likelihoods of e under H and its rivals. How H came to be entertained is irrelevant unless it changes those quantities.

Error statisticians affirm predictivism for an important class of cases (Mayo 1996, 2018; Mayo and Cox 2006). Suppose a hypothesis is hunted out of a large space because it fits. The procedure that produced the fit would have produced some fit or other whether or not its output was true. A passing result from such a procedure therefore has little probative force.

Particle physicists build the second view into practice. Under the look-elsewhere effect, a bump found by scanning a mass range is assessed by a *global* significance. The global significance is weaker than the *local* significance, which is computed as if the mass had been fixed in advance (Gross and Vitells 2010).

I restrict attention to *selection cases*. In these, a publicly specified search S picks a hypothesis from a space Ω because of its fit to data e. The thesis has three parts.

**(T1) Total invariance.** The total confirmation e gives the selected hypothesis H, and hence H's posterior, does not depend on whether H was selected by S or proposed in advance, holding fixed the agent's credences over hypotheses and data.

**(T2) Selection partition.** The search fixes a privileged factorization of that total into two factors:
- the confirmation H receives from the bare fact that S selected it;
- the confirmation H receives *beyond* selection.

The second factor, *selection-relative support*, does depend on history. In searches over large, undifferentiated spaces it falls short of the total by a large factor, the *reach* of the search.

**(T3) Allocation.** The selection adjustments that predictivists and error statisticians make are correct when read as verdicts about H relative to the selection event: about selection-relative support, together with the credibility that selection itself confers. Read as verdicts about total support, they are incorrect. Under symmetry, selection-relative support equals the confirmation of the outcome-indexed proposition "whatever S returns is true." That is why these verdicts are naturally phrased about the search's output.

This is a Bayesian view, not a neutral reconciliation. It rejects predictivism about total support. Most Bayesian treatments place the predictivist intuition somewhere other than H's support:
- in the predictor's reliability (Maher 1988; White 2003);
- in accommodation's tendency to yield arbitrary or fudged theories (Lange 2001; Lipton 2004);
- in overfitting (Hitchcock and Sober 2004).

The present view differs. It identifies a support relation for H itself, relative to a principled background, on which the history of selection matters. In the terms of Hitchcock and Sober (2004) and Barnes (2008), it rejects strong predictivism about total support and defends a relativized predictivism about the same content.

The central formula, (2) below, has a statistical counterpart in selection-adjusted likelihoods for selected parameters (Yekutieli 2012). It is also consistent with Dawid's (1994) observation that data-dependent selection leaves Bayesian posteriors unaffected. My contribution is philosophical. I offer:
- a criterion that fixes which part of the evidence counts as "used," answering a question that use-novelty accounts left open;
- an argument that error-statistical selection adjustments track the resulting partition;
- a diagnosis of "nominal" error probabilities as double counting.

## 2. Setup

Let Ω = {H₁, …, Hₙ} be mutually exclusive hypotheses. There may be a residual possibility H₀, such as "no signal." Let E be the random data, with values e.

A search S is a function, known to the agent, from data values to Ω ∪ {⊥}. Here ⊥ means "no report," as when nothing crosses a threshold. Let Rep = [S(E) ≠ ⊥]. In the actual case S(e) = H. Section 9 relaxes the assumption that S is known.

The **selection event** is A = [S(E) = H] = S⁻¹(H). The actual data entail A.

The **outcome-indexed proposition** is σ = ⋃ᵢ [S(E) = Hᵢ ∧ Hᵢ], the proposition that the search reports some hypothesis and that hypothesis is true.

σ is a fixed set of worlds. What varies across worlds is which Hᵢ it agrees with. The contrast with the rigid H is the contrast between "the lottery winner is from Boston" and "Smith is from Boston," said when Smith won. It resembles the contrast between a diagonal proposition and a horizontal one. I avoid the labels "de re" and "de dicto," which concern the scope of attitude and modal operators.

Confirmation is measured by the Bayes factor B(X, e) = O(X | e)/O(X). B(X, e | Y) is the same ratio computed relative to background that includes Y. For binary hypotheses, B(H, e) equals the likelihood ratio LR_e(H) = P(e | H)/P(e | ¬H). Section 4 addresses measure-dependence.

## 3. The selection partition

Since e entails A, the chain rule for odds gives

  (1) B(H, e) = B(H, A) · B(H, e | A),

or equivalently,

  (2) B(H, e | A) = LR_e(H) / LR_A(H).

I call B(H, e | A) **selection-relative support**.

Formula (2) shows where the procedure enters, and it respects the likelihood principle. The total import of e for H is LR_e(H), which does not depend on S. That is the Bayesian's point, and the account keeps it. What S determines is which data values make up A, and therefore how the fixed total divides between "being selected" and "beyond selection." Yekutieli's (2012) adjusted likelihood is the same construction for parameter inference: the sampling density divided by the probability of selection given the parameter.

### 3.1 Why A?

Two objections arise at once.

The first: *any* decomposition e = X ∧ R yields B(H, e) = B(H, X) · B(H, R | X). So (1) is privileged only if A has some independent claim to be the "used" part of e.

The second: making a part of the evidence into background is old-evidence territory (Glymour 1980; Howson 1991; Christensen 1999). The use-novelty tradition never settled which aspects of the data count as "used" (Zahar 1973; Gardner 1982; Worrall 1985, 1989, 2002).

My criterion is this. **A is the fibre of S through e: the coarsest data-determined event that settles which hypothesis the procedure puts forward.** It is privileged for three reasons.

*(i) Presupposition.* The question "how strongly does the evidence support the hypothesis this analysis put forward?" presupposes that the analysis put forward H. It presupposes nothing stronger about e. An answer to a question is ordinarily evaluated against the question's presuppositions, so this question is answered by B(H, e | A). By contrast, B(H, e) answers "how strongly does e support H?" as asked by someone who picked out H independently. The two numbers answer two questions about one hypothesis.

*(ii) Guaranteed fit.* For an always-reporting search, ⋃ᵢ S⁻¹(Hᵢ) is certain. A is the part of the evidence that the procedure guarantees some hypothesis will fit. This makes the error statistician's "it would have passed anyway" precise. What would have happened anyway is A-type agreement, so its contribution is set aside.

*(iii) Public determinability.* A is fixed by S and its output. Analyst and reader can both compute it. Use-novelty's "aspects used in construction" cannot be computed in this way.

The criterion also defuses a Popper–Miller-style worry (Popper and Miller 1983; Jeffrey 1984; Redhead 1985). Indefinitely many propositions X satisfy X ∧ e ≡ H ∧ e, and by moving prior mass among ¬e-worlds their confirmation can be made almost anything. If the thesis ranked such propositions by confirmation, the ranking would be arbitrary. But (T2) concerns H alone. Only the background varies, and it is fixed by a criterion stated before any confirmation is computed. The proposition σ enters only as a reformulation in the symmetric case, and even there it is defined from S before the data, not built from e.

### 3.2 One content, two histories

Predictivism, properly stated, says that *the same content* is supported differently under different histories. Consider a theorist who announces H before the data. The event that fixes the referent is A_T = [the theorist announced H], which is not a function of e.

Suppose the announcement is probabilistically independent of the data given each hypothesis. Then B(H, e | A_T) = LR_e(H) = B(H, e). So for the predicted H, selection-relative support equals total support. For the accommodated H, it falls short by the factor B(H, A).

The same proposition, H, receives the same total support and different selection-relative support. That difference is the relativized predictivism (T2) asserts.

## 4. Symmetric searches and the outcome-indexed proposition

**Proposition 1.** P(σ | e) = P(H | e).

*Proof.* The data e entail A, and σ ∧ A ≡ H ∧ A. ∎

No coherent agent with evidence e can therefore assign different credences to σ and H. The difference between them lies in their priors, and so in their confirmation.

**Proposition 2.** Assume two symmetry conditions.
- (i) The agent's joint credence over hypotheses and data is invariant under any relabelling of Ω's indices applied jointly to hypotheses and data. This constrains the likelihoods (backgrounds, resolution, efficiency) as well as the prior.
- (ii) S is equivariant.

Then O(H | A) = O(σ | Rep), and B(H, e | A) = B(σ, e | Rep). If S always reports, these become O(H | A) = O(σ) and B(H, e | A) = B(σ, e).

*Proof.* By symmetry, P(A) = P(Rep)/n. Since σ entails Rep, symmetry gives P(H ∧ A) = P(σ)/n, so P(H | A) = P(σ | Rep). Because σ ∧ A ≡ H ∧ A and e entails both A and Rep, Proposition 1 gives B(H, e | A) = O(σ | e)/O(σ | Rep) = B(σ, e | Rep). ∎

Under symmetry, then, selection-relative support is the confirmation of the proposition that the search's report is correct. Define the **reach factor** as

  (3) ρ = B(H, A) = O(σ | Rep)/O(H).

Under symmetry, P(σ | A) = P(σ | Rep). Learning *which* hypothesis was selected confirms H by ρ but says nothing about whether the search succeeded.

Several properties of ρ follow.
- For an always-reporting search with signal probability P(∃), uniform location and power π, we have P(H) = P(∃)/n and P(σ) = P(∃)·π. So ρ is roughly nπ when P(H) is small.
- Hence ρ > 1 exactly when the search does better than a random pick.
- At fixed signal strength, π falls as n grows, because the maximum of n noise cells grows roughly as √(2 log n). So ρ grows sublinearly in n. A value "in the hundreds" for a thousand cells reflects an assumed power, not a law.
- In general, selection-relative support exceeds total support only if B(H, A) < 1, that is, only if being selected counts *against* H. That requires asymmetry, for example a search biased towards a region the agent disfavours. The account predicts such reversals, but I know of no practice against which to test the prediction.

**Measure robustness.** Relative to background A, H's prior is P(H | A) and its posterior is still P(H | e). The difference measure d, the ratio measure r, the likelihood measure l (the Bayes factor) and Crupi, Tentori and Gonzalez's (2007) z all decrease as the prior rises with the posterior held fixed. So the ordinal claim holds on each of them: selection-relative support falls below total support whenever B(H, A) > 1. The multiplicative form of (1), and the value of ρ, are specific to l (Fitelson 1999).

## 5. A worked case

Consider a scan for a narrow resonance across n = 1000 resolution cells.
- The prior that some resonance lies in the window is P(∃) = 0.5, with uniform location, so P(Hᵢ) = 0.0005.
- S always reports the cell with the largest local excess.
- If a resonance exists, S finds its cell with probability 0.6, so P(σ) = 0.3.
- The symmetry conditions hold.
- The largest excess falls in cell k, and the data are strong enough that P(H_k | e) = 0.8, with negligible posterior mass on resonances in other cells.

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| O(H_k) | ≈ 0.0005 |
| O(H_k \| A) = O(σ) | ≈ 0.43 |
| Reach factor ρ = B(H_k, A) | ≈ 857 |
| O(H_k \| e) = O(σ \| e) | 4 |
| Total support B(H_k, e) | ≈ 8000 |
| Selection-relative support B(H_k, e \| A) = B(σ, e) | ≈ 9.3 |

These numbers describe a strong local excess with only modest global significance. A 5σ local excess in a thousand cells would yield selection-relative support in the thousands.

Learning only that the maximum fell in cell k raises the credence in a resonance there from 1 in 2000 to 3 in 10. Of the total factor of 8000, about 860 comes from k's being where the maximum fell, which was bound to be true of some cell. About 9 is support beyond selection.

Now suppose a theorist chose cell k by lottery and announced it in advance. Total support is still 8000, and by §3.2 selection-relative support is also 8000. The proposition is the same, and the two histories agree in total support and disagree in selection-relative support. The source of the disagreement is that "the bump fell in the announced cell" was improbable unless the theorist was right, whereas "the bump fell in the search's cell" was certain either way.

The slogan "it would have looked this good anyway" is ambiguous. It is false relative to the rigid H_k: without a resonance there, cell k would very probably not show this excess. It is true of the search's output: had that output been spurious, some cell would very probably still have shown an excess this large.

**Tail areas.** It is tempting to read local and global p-values as the denominators of these likelihood ratios. That reading is loose. Bayes factors computed for the exact datum can differ by orders of magnitude from those computed for tail events (Berger and Sellke 1987). The correct statement concerns coarsened evidence. Let π = [Z_max ≥ z].

- In worlds where H_k is false, cell k is pure noise, so P(Z_k ≥ z | ¬H_k) is the local p-value.
- In worlds where σ is false, either there is no resonance, or there is one in cell j that the search missed. In the second case, a false pass requires some noise cell i ≠ j to exceed z. If cells are independent and a narrow resonance leaves other cells' noise unchanged, that probability is at most the probability that the maximum of n noise cells exceeds z, which is the global p-value.

So the background-only hypothesis is the least favourable case. The global p-value bounds P(π | ¬σ), the false-pass probability that forms the denominator of the coarsened selection-relative support.

## 6. Objections from total evidence and the look-elsewhere effect

**(O1) Total evidence.** After the search, the agent knows e and that S returned H, so σ and H are equivalent for her. On this objection, any discount that comes from averaging over what S could have returned is a pre-data error rate, and contrasting it with the posterior merely restates the Bayesian/error-statistical dispute.

Reply. Proposition 1 grants the equivalence. Selection-relative support is not a pre-data error rate. B(H, e | A) is a post-data confirmation of H relative to background the agent actually has. Its only procedural ingredients, P(A | H) and P(A | ¬H), are likelihoods of an event she observed.

Averaging over possible outputs appears only in P(σ), and only as a reformulation of P(H | A) under symmetry. The objection's recommended move, conditioning on "S returned H," is exactly what produces selection-relative support once we ask about support rather than credence. Nor is this the dispute restated: the account sides with the Bayesian on total support, which is what that dispute is about.

**(O2) The look-elsewhere dilemma.** In Bayesian treatments of mass scans the trials factor reappears as an Occam factor. The objection takes this factor to attach to the rigid "resonance at m₀," which yields a dilemma:
- either the penalty sits in the rigid hypothesis's prior, which contradicts (T1);
- or the global p-value has no credal counterpart.

First horn. The rigid prior is indeed diluted. But the dilution represents the ignorance that made a search necessary; it is not a penalty for searching. The lottery theorist faces the same dilution, the same total support and the same posterior. Where advance proposal raises the prior, as when a mass is derived from an electroweak fit, the posterior differs because of the theorist's reasons. That is a separate mechanism (§9).

Second horn. The standard calculation compares a composite alternative, "a resonance somewhere in the window," with background-only (Cousins 2017). Its Bayes factor is roughly the maximized likelihood ratio multiplied by an Occam factor of order δm/Δm, the resolution divided by the window width. The rigid point hypothesis carries no such factor. The penalty therefore attaches to the existential hypothesis ∃. That point is standard, and I claim no novelty for it.

In the example, B(∃, e) ≈ 4. This differs from B(σ, e) ≈ 9.3 by O(∃)/O(σ) ≈ 2.3, which depends on both P(∃) and power. In the scan, ∃ does most of the work that σ does. The bearing of the existential/specific contrast on the look-elsewhere effect has been discussed by R. Dawid (2015) and Staley (2017).

The partition adds three things.

1. It explains why the claim physicists actually report inherits the existential discount. That claim is a localized one, "a new boson with mass near 125 GeV," and once stated it is rigid. The existential hypothesis says nothing about the mass. The localized claim is discounted because it is being evaluated relative to its selection event.
2. It extends to selection cases that have no natural existential surrogate. Examples are search over non-nested models, and subgroup selection where what is acted on is "this subgroup benefits," not "some subgroup does."
3. It accounts for the global p-value's object. Formally it tests ¬∃. By §5, background-only is the least favourable case for a false pass, so the global p-value also bounds the search's error about its own output.

## 7. Reporting and reliance: background matching

If total and selection-relative support assign the same posterior, why should it matter which one is reported? The answer depends on who combines the reported figure with which prior.

**Background matching (BM).** A support figure reported for combination with a reader's prior must be computed relative to whatever background that prior already incorporates. Otherwise evidence is counted twice or not at all.

Three kinds of reader illustrate the principle.

*Readers with a full model.* A reader with a prior over Ω and a model of S can use the reported likelihood function directly. For her, no selection-relative figure is needed. I grant this.

*Readers with track-record base rates.* Many readers have no model of S but hold a calibrated sense of how often hypotheses that this kind of analysis puts forward turn out true. That is an estimate of P(H | A) for the class, which under symmetry equals P(σ | Rep). It is a coherent conditional credence; what the reader lacks is the model that generates it. By BM such a reader needs B(H, e | A). If she combines the total support with her base rate, she counts A twice. In the example she would reach posterior odds of 0.43 × 8000 ≈ 3400 instead of 4.

*Readers with post-threshold base rates.* Some readers' base rates are positive predictive values of reported discoveries at a threshold (Ioannidis 2005). This is why the formal model lets S return ⊥. In a threshold procedure, A entails that the threshold was crossed, so P(H | A) *is* the positive predictive value at that threshold, and BM calls for B(H, e | A) with that A.

If a base rate conditions on more than A, for example on the realized significance, BM requires backgrounding that information as well. A base rate conditioned on the exact datum leaves no further support to report.

The general formulation thus blocks double counting in both directions. The always-report formula B(σ, e) would misfire for threshold-conditioned readers, which is one reason it is not the general explicans.

Two qualifications follow.

First, I do not claim that science always transmits support rather than posteriors. BM applies when a report is meant to be combined with readers' priors.

Second, a global p-value is not a support measure, and it cannot be multiplied by a prior. Its role in a frequentist report parallels that of B(H, e | A) in a Bayesian one: it ensures that the credited evidence excludes the selection event.

On this reading, the dual local and global significances reported in the 2012 Higgs announcements answer two questions. One concerns readers who identified the mass independently. The other concerns readers who meet it as the search's output.

**Reliance.** Institutional rules have the form "act on outputs of P when T ≥ c." Such a rule is good or bad according to P(σ | T ≥ c), weighted by stakes, whether it is assessed by expected utility or by error rates. That is a selection-conditioned quantity by construction.

**Replication.** New data e′ are assessed relative to background e, which already contains A. No new selection occurs, so for e′ there is nothing to partition, and its support passes undiscounted to readers whatever their background. H thereby detaches from its description as "the search's output." This is why replication matters so much in practice, even though the original data already gave H strong total support.

## 8. Error statistics: what selection adjustments track

**(O3) Misattribution.** Mayo holds that the hunted H itself has passed a test of low capacity. Telling her that she is right about something else attributes to her a view she rejects.

I agree that she would reject the gloss. My claim is that her selection-sensitive verdicts are true only on it, and that her actual computations follow it.

**Nominal error probabilities as double counting.** An error-statistical evaluation of a selected hypothesis treats it as the procedure's output. Its starting point is therefore the procedure's reliability, which in credal terms is P(H | A). The "nominal" error probability, computed as though H had been fixed in advance, is the local probability. It belongs to the total support of the rigid H.

Combining a selection-conditioned starting point with total support counts A twice. That is the frequentist analogue of the reader's mistake in §7. The "actual" error probability (Mayo and Cox 2006) corrects this by taking support relative to A.

On this diagnosis, hunting cases and harmless use-construction share a single structure.

*Hunting.* In the scan, selection confers modest credibility: P(H_k | A) = 0.3. The verdict therefore depends on support beyond selection, which is weak. The global error probability is the frequentist measure of that support.

*Harmless use-construction.* Let S map the sample mean (with σ known) to the interval x̄ ± 1.96σ/√m. Then A = [X̄ = x̄] exhausts the sufficient evidence, so B(H, e | A) = 1 and there is no support beyond selection. But selection is itself reliable. Coverage gives P(σ) = 0.95 under every prior, and P(H | A) ≈ 0.95 under a flat one.

Mayo judges this use-construction harmless, and her verdict tracks the 0.05 error rate. Its credal counterpart is the high selection-conditioned credibility. Her verdict credits nothing beyond A. The nominal computation would ask how rarely the data would fit [a, b] so well were μ outside it. That would credit the fit a second time, and it is precisely the computation she declines.

The two cases share an object, H relative to A. They differ in which component carries the verdict. Severity verdicts are therefore not pure increment verdicts. In the estimator case the verdict rests on a firmness-like component, and §4's focus on support should be read with that qualification.

The claim is not merely that error-statistical numbers "are about the procedure," which no one disputes. The claim is more specific:
- it identifies which Bayesian quantity each adjustment corresponds to;
- it explains why the nominal computation is an error;
- it explains why use-construction is harmful in one case and harmless in the other.

I have not found a single credal quantity that reproduces every severity verdict. Coarsening to tail events (§5) is a further feature of error-statistical practice that this account does not reconstruct.

**The rigid reading, and a criticism.** Suppose the test H_k passed is taken to be the hunting procedure, and the counterfactual is read rigidly: had H_k been false, the procedure would very probably have output something else. On that reading severity is high, so Mayo cannot locate low severity there. Her low-severity verdict is true only of H evaluated relative to its selection.

The inference she then draws, that x₀ is poor evidence for H, is valid for selection-relative support and invalid for total support. I take this as a substantive criticism. "Evidence for H" in severity reasoning is ambiguous between the two, and the hunting verdicts are true only on the relativized reading.

## 9. Scope and limits

**Publicly specified searches.** The construction requires S to be a known function, so that e entails A and the reader can compute LR_A. In forking-paths cases (Gelman and Loken 2014) the reader does not know S.

The partition generalizes: the referent-fixing event becomes "the analyst reported H." Its likelihoods, however, now depend on the reader's credence over possible procedures, and selection-relative support becomes correspondingly indeterminate.

The two remedies practitioners use make this indeterminacy disappear.
- Pre-registration makes the referent-fixing event data-independent, as in §3.2, so selection-relative support equals total support.
- Holdout data keep the evidence that fixes the referent separate from the evidence being assessed.

I claim only that this fits the remedies, not that it is their sole justification.

**Asymmetric searches.** Real scans are asymmetric. Backgrounds fall with mass, resolution and efficiency vary across the window, and theoretical priors are not uniform. In such cases Proposition 2 fails, P(σ | A) may differ from P(σ | Rep), and the outcome-indexed formulation becomes at best a heuristic. B(H, e | A) remains well defined, and it is the general thesis. The rigid/outcome-indexed contrast is the special case under symmetry.

**Non-selection predictivism.** In Maher's (1988) and White's (2003) cases, the prediction comes before the data, and the advantage arises because a successful prediction is evidence of the predictor's reliability. A theorist's choice is a selection from a space, but it is not a selection *by the evidence being assessed*. The referent-fixing event A_T is not a function of e. In those cases the predictivist effect enters through what A_T and e indicate about the theorist, and it changes total support. Ordinary conditioning handles this, and it lies outside the present account.

**Related accounts.** Side-effect accounts (Lange 2001; Lipton 2004) and Bayesian treatments of selection effects in likelihood reasoning (Kotzen 2012) are complementary to this one. Overfitting arguments (Hitchcock and Sober 2004) concern the predictive accuracy of the output of a fitting procedure. A natural extension would treat that accuracy as a selection-conditioned property. I do not pursue it here.

## 10. Conclusion

In selection cases, the selected hypothesis and the proposition that the search's output is true are equally probable on the total evidence. Their posteriors cannot carry a predictivist discount. Support can.

The search fixes a privileged partition of the evidence into the selection event and the rest. The selection event is the coarsest data-determined event that settles which hypothesis is put forward. Total support factors into the confirmation from selection and the support beyond it.

Total support is history-invariant, and there the Bayesian is right. Support beyond selection is history-dependent for one and the same hypothesis, and there the predictivist is right. Under symmetry it equals the confirmation of "whatever the search returns is true."

Error-statistical selection adjustments, the physicists' global significance, and the Bayesian Occam factor all operate on the selection-relative side. "Nominal" error probabilities pair a selection-conditioned starting point with total support, and so count the selection twice. Mayo's step from low severity to "poor evidence for H" is sound when "evidence" means support beyond selection, and unsound when it means total support.

The argument needs a bridge principle from question presupposition to confirmational background, and none is offered. A is the fibre of S, so it depends on (i) the grain of Omega, (ii) what counts as S's output, and (iii) the scope of S. On (ii), outputting 'the max cell' and 'the max cell plus the set of cells above threshold' give different fibres for the same physical analysis. On (iii), one mass window, several decay channels, or all analyses run by a collaboration give different searches. Since rho is roughly n*pi, grain choices move selection-relative support by orders of magnitude. Granularity also bites inside the model. With resolution cells and correlated neighbours, the commonest 'miss' is picking cell j+1 when the resonance is at j. That counts as sigma false, which makes 'power' and hence rho sensitive to an arbitrary binning. The paper needs an account of which description of S fixes A, or an argument that its conclusions are robust across admissible descriptions.
